title: Fish and Chips
subtitle: Beer-battered cod with thick-cut chips
excerpt: British fish and chips done properly: cod fillets in a crisp, light beer batter fried until shatteringly crunchy and golden, alongside thick-cut potatoes twice-fried for fluffy middles and crisp exteriors. Serve with vinegar, mushy peas, and tartare sauce.

recipe.sourceNotes: Fish and chips emerged in Britain in the 1860s when frying fish (brought by Sephardic Jewish immigrants from Portugal and Spain) combined with fried potatoes (introduced separately, possibly from Belgium or France). By the early twentieth century the dish had become one of the staples of the British working-class diet, sold from dedicated shops called chippies. The batter uses beer or sparkling water: the carbon dioxide creates bubbles that expand in the heat, giving a light, airy coating that does not become greasy. The double-fry method for the chips (first at lower temperature to cook through, then at high temperature for colour and crispness) is the key technique for achieving the classic result. Good fish and chips requires a thermometer; temperature control is everything.

recipeTools.notes: Oil temperature is critical. Too low and the batter absorbs oil; too high and it darkens before the fish cooks through.

content.text: The batter must be cold and the oil must be hot. Make the batter at the last moment using very cold beer; add ice cubes to the bowl if needed. Do not overmix; a few lumps are fine and produce a lighter result. Dry the fish thoroughly before battering or the coating will slide off.

items.preparation: 4 fillets, skin removed and thoroughly dried with kitchen paper
Maris Piper or King Edward; peeled and cut into 1.5 cm chips
very cold lager or pale ale

content.text: Blanch the chips in a large pan of salted water for 5 minutes. Drain thoroughly and spread on a tray to cool and dry completely. Heat the oil in a large, deep pan to 130°C. Fry the blanched chips in batches for 5 minutes until cooked through but not coloured. Drain and set aside.
Make the batter just before frying: whisk the flour, baking powder, and a pinch of salt. Whisk in the cold beer until a smooth batter forms; a few small lumps are fine. Keep cold.

Increase the oil to 180°C. Dust the fish fillets in flour, shaking off the excess. Dip into the batter and lower into the oil, holding for a few seconds before releasing so the batter sets. Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper.

While the fish cooks, return the oil to 190°C and fry the blanched chips in batches for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and very crisp. Drain, salt immediately, and serve alongside the fish with malt vinegar.
